lessons.unit: Spring 1: States of matter (Marvellous Medicine and How Far Can Sound Travel?)
lessons.title: Solids, liquids and gases
lessons.bigQuestion: How can we tell if something is a solid, a liquid or a gas?
objectives: To understand how solids, liquids and gases are different
successCriteria: All: sort materials into solids, liquids and gases
Most: describe one property of each state
Some: explain where tricky materials such as sand belong
lessons.crossCurricular: English: using 'because' to justify a choice
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: wonder at how one substance, water, can take three forms

keywords.def: keeps its own shape and does not flow
flows and takes the shape of its container
spreads out to fill any space
whether something is a solid, liquid or gas
the amount of space something takes up

hook.text: Is sand a solid or a liquid? It pours like water. What do you think, and why?
hook.a: A solid: each grain keeps its shape. It pours because the grains are tiny.

islamicLink.text: Allah says: 'We made from water every living thing' (al-Anbiya 21:30). Water is the only substance we meet every day as a solid, a liquid and a gas, and every living thing needs it.

starter.q: Is wood a solid or a liquid?

teach.heading: Three states
bullets: Materials can be solid, liquid or gas
teach.note: Show an ice cube and a cup of water. Ask: what is the same? Both are water.

teach.heading: Solids and liquids
bullets: Liquids flow and can be poured
Liquids take the shape of the container
teach.note: Pour water into a tall glass and a bowl on camera: the shape changes, the amount stays the same.

teach.heading: Gases
bullets: Gases spread to fill any space
teach.note: Squash an air-filled plastic bag: it pushes back. Smell from cooking spreads through the house: a gas spreading.

teach.heading: Sort them
teach.note: Read each card; pupils hold up 1, 2 or 3 fingers.

practice.q: Is honey a solid or a liquid?
practice.a: A liquid: it flows (slowly) and takes the shape of its container.
practice.model:
Ask: does it keep its shape?
No.
Does it flow?
Yes, slowly.
Things that flow are liquids.
So honey is a liquid.

practice.q: Why is sand a solid even though it pours?
practice.a: Each grain is a tiny solid that keeps its own shape.

practice.q: Which state can be squashed easily?

independent.q: Core: Make a three-column table (solid, liquid, gas). Add four things from your home to each column.
independent.a: For example: solid: spoon, table, rice, soap; liquid: water, oil, juice, vinegar; gas: air, steam, the air in a ball, cooking smells.
independent.model: Teacher does one of each first: spoon (solid, keeps its shape), oil (liquid, pours), air in a balloon (gas, fills the space).

independent.q: Extend: Write one sentence for each state starting 'A ... is ... because ...'
independent.a: For example: A spoon is a solid because it keeps its shape.

independent.q: Stretch: Is toothpaste a solid or a liquid? Give your reasons.
independent.a: Accept a reasoned answer: it flows when squeezed (like a liquid) but holds its shape on the brush (like a solid).

exit.q: Which state spreads out to fill any space?
exit.a: Gas

exit.q: Big question: how can we tell if something is a solid, a liquid or a gas?
exit.a: Solids keep their shape; liquids flow and take the container's shape; gases spread out to fill any space.

lessons.homework: Find ten materials around your home and sort them into solid, liquid or gas in a table.
lessons.send: SEND: picture cards to sort; allow pointing. EAL: solid, liquid, gas with pictures. Stretch: explain why a balloon gets bigger when you blow into it.

lessons.title: Water in three states: observing ice, water and steam
lessons.bigQuestion: Is ice still water?
objectives: To understand that water can change between solid, liquid and gas and stay the same substance
successCriteria: All: name ice, water and water vapour as the three states of water
Most: describe what we see as ice melts and water boils
Some: explain that steam we see is tiny water droplets and water vapour is invisible
lessons.crossCurricular: Geography: water in rivers, ice at the poles and clouds
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: gratitude for water, a mercy from Allah

keywords.def: water as a solid
water as a gas; it is invisible
the mist of tiny water drops above boiling water
look carefully and notice
when a material turns from one state to another

hook.text: You see a white cloud above a boiling kettle. Is that cloud a gas?
hook.a: Not quite: the cloud is tiny water drops. The gas (water vapour) is invisible, just at the spout.

islamicLink.text: Allah says: 'Have you seen the water that you drink? Is it you who brought it down from the clouds, or are We the One who sends it down?' (al-Waqi'ah 56:68-69). The same water moves between ice, liquid and vapour, and Allah sends it back to us as rain.

starter.q: Is milk a solid, liquid or gas?
Name one property of a gas.
starter.a: For example: it spreads to fill a space; it can be squashed.

teach.heading: One substance, three states
teach.note: Show an ice cube melting on a plate on camera.

teach.heading: Watch a kettle (teacher only)
teach.note: Teacher demonstrates on camera. Point out the clear gap at the spout: invisible water vapour.

teach.heading: What we observe
bullets: Ice: hard, cold, keeps its shape
Water: flows, takes the cup's shape
teach.note: Model good observation words: 'I notice...'

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: 30 seconds.

check.q: Water vapour is...
check.why: Water vapour is invisible. The white cloud is tiny liquid drops that have cooled.

practice.q: What state is ice?
practice.model:
Ask: does ice keep its shape?
Yes.
Things that keep their shape are solids.
So ice is a solid.

practice.q: What happens to an ice cube left on a warm plate?
Is the steam cloud we see a gas?
practice.a: No, it is tiny drops of liquid water; the gas is invisible.

independent.q: Core: Put an ice cube on a saucer. Observe it every 5 minutes for 15 minutes. Write what you notice each time.
independent.a: For example: 0 min hard and dry; 5 min a puddle forming; 10 min smaller and rounder; 15 min mostly water.
independent.model:
Teacher shows the first observation: 'At 0 minutes the ice is hard, cold and has sharp edges.
There is no water on the saucer.'

independent.q: Extend: Draw the three states of water and label each one.
independent.a: Ice (solid), water (liquid), water vapour (gas).

independent.q: Stretch: Where in nature do we find water as a solid, a liquid and a gas?
independent.a: Solid: glaciers, snow; liquid: rivers, sea, rain; gas: water vapour in the air.

exit.q: Ice is water as a...
exit.a: A) solid

exit.q: Big question: is ice still water?
exit.a: Yes: it is the same substance in a different state.

lessons.homework: With an adult, find water in all three states at home (ice in the freezer, water from a tap, vapour from a kettle or a hot bath) and write one sentence about each.
lessons.send: SEND: observation sheet with picture prompts. EAL: melt, ice, vapour with gestures. Stretch: explain why ice melts faster in a warm room.

lessons.title: Changes of state: melting and freezing
lessons.bigQuestion: Why does chocolate melt in your hand but not in the fridge?
objectives: To understand that heating melts solids and cooling freezes liquids
successCriteria: All: sort changes into melting or freezing
Most: give the melting point of ice as 0 °C
Some: explain why different materials melt at different temperatures
lessons.crossCurricular: Design and technology: melting chocolate and setting jelly in cooking
lessons.smsc: Moral: taking care around hot things and helping adults safely in the kitchen

keywords.def: change from a solid to a liquid by heating
change from a liquid to a solid by cooling
warm something up
the temperature at which a solid melts
the unit for temperature, written °C

hook.text: Butter, chocolate and ice all melt. Which do you think melts first on a warm day, and why?
hook.a: Ice and butter melt at lower temperatures than most chocolate; each material has its own melting point.

starter.q: Name the three states of water.

teach.heading: Melting
bullets: Heating a solid can melt it
teach.note: Ask: what makes ice melt faster? Warmth.

teach.heading: Freezing
bullets: Cooling a liquid can freeze it
teach.note: Ice lollies and ice cubes: liquid put in a freezer.

teach.heading: Melting points differ
bullets: Each material melts at its own temperature
teach.note: These are approximate values.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: 30 seconds.

check.q: Liquid water is put in a freezer. What happens?
check.why: Cooling a liquid makes it freeze into a solid.

practice.q: Chocolate in a warm hand. Melting or freezing?
practice.model:
Is it being heated or cooled?
The hand is warm, so heated.
Heating a solid makes it melt.
So it is melting.

practice.q: Juice put in a freezer. What happens?
practice.a: It freezes into a solid (ice lolly).

practice.q: At what temperature does ice melt?

independent.q: Core: Put a small piece of butter, chocolate and ice on three saucers in the same warm place. Which melts first? Record your order.
independent.a: Usually ice first, then butter, then chocolate; accept pupils' own careful observations.
independent.model: Teacher sets up all three on camera: same size pieces, same place, start the timer together.

independent.q: Extend: Use the chart to explain your order.
independent.a: Materials with lower melting points melt first at the same temperature.

independent.q: Stretch: Why does a candle melt near the flame but stay solid at the bottom?
independent.a: Only the wax near the flame reaches its melting point (about 60 °C).

exit.q: Heating a solid can make it...
exit.a: B) melt

exit.q: Big question: why does chocolate melt in your hand but not in the fridge?
exit.a: Your hand is warmer than its melting point; the fridge is colder.

lessons.homework: Make a list of three things in your kitchen that melt and three that freeze.
lessons.send: SEND: real ice and chocolate, picture word mat. EAL: melt, freeze, heat, cool. Stretch: find out the melting point of another material and add it to the chart.

lessons.title: Measuring temperature: where does ice melt fastest?
lessons.bigQuestion: Where in your home would an ice cube melt fastest?
objectives: To understand how to measure temperature and use it to explain how fast ice melts
successCriteria: All: read a thermometer in degrees Celsius
Most: run a fair test of ice melting in different places
Some: explain the link between temperature and melting time
lessons.crossCurricular: Maths: reading scales and negative numbers
lessons.smsc: Social: sharing results fairly and listening to other groups

keywords.def: how hot or cold something is
a tool that measures temperature
the unit for temperature, written °C
a test where we change only one thing
say what you think will happen

hook.text: A freezer, a fridge and a sunny windowsill. Put them in order from coldest to warmest. How could you check?
hook.a: Freezer, fridge, windowsill. Check with a thermometer.

starter.a: Changing from a solid to a liquid by heating.

starter.q: In a fair test, how many things do we change?

teach.heading: Reading a thermometer
bullets: Read the number by the top of the liquid or on the screen
teach.note: Show a kitchen thermometer on camera. Model reading 21 °C.

teach.heading: Our fair test
bullets: Same: size of ice cube, same saucer
teach.note: Ask: what must stay the same?

teach.heading: Example results
teach.note: Discuss the pattern.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: 30 seconds.

check.q: Which place melted ice fastest?
check.why: It was warmest near the radiator (35 °C), so the ice melted in 15 minutes.

practice.q: Read the table: how long did ice take to melt on the kitchen table?
practice.model:
Find the row 'Kitchen table'.
Look across to the column 'Time to melt'.
It says 40.
So 40 minutes.

practice.q: What is the pattern?
practice.a: The higher the temperature, the shorter the melting time.

practice.q: Normal body temperature is about...

independent.q: Core: Place three equal ice cubes on saucers in three places at home (one in the fridge). Check every 10 minutes. Record which melts first.
independent.a: Pupils' own; the warmest place melts first.
independent.model: Teacher shows the setup: same tray of ice cubes, label each saucer, write the start time.

independent.q: Extend: Write a conclusion: 'The ice melted fastest ... because ...'
independent.a: For example: The ice melted fastest by the window because it was the warmest place.

independent.q: Stretch: Why is the temperature in a fridge useful for keeping food fresh?
independent.a: It is cold (about 4 °C), which slows down the growth of germs.

exit.q: Temperature is measured in...
exit.a: B) degrees Celsius

exit.q: Big question: where in your home would an ice cube melt fastest?
exit.a: The warmest place, because a higher temperature melts ice faster.

lessons.homework: Finish your ice test and write your conclusion. If you have a thermometer, record the temperature of each place.
lessons.send: SEND: a big-print number line for reading temperatures. EAL: hot, warm, cold, temperature. Stretch: plot the example results as a bar chart.

lessons.title: Evaporation: where does the water go?
lessons.bigQuestion: Where does a puddle go on a sunny day?
objectives: To understand that evaporation turns liquid water into water vapour
successCriteria: All: say that water evaporates and becomes water vapour
Most: name things that make evaporation faster
Some: explain why washing dries faster on a warm, windy day
lessons.crossCurricular: Geography: drying of rivers and lakes in hot countries
lessons.smsc: Moral: not wasting water, which Allah gives us

keywords.def: when a liquid turns into a gas
water as an invisible gas
with no water left
how fast something happens
warm something up

hook.text: Wet washing on a line slowly dries. The water does not drip onto the ground. Where does it go?
hook.a: It evaporates into the air as invisible water vapour.

islamicLink.text: Allah says: 'And We sent down from the sky water in due measure and settled it in the earth' (al-Mu'minun 23:18). Evaporation is part of how Allah moves water from the ground and sea back up to the clouds.

starter.a: A solid changing to a liquid when heated.

starter.q: At what temperature does ice melt?

teach.heading: Evaporation
bullets: Liquid water turns into water vapour
teach.note: Wipe a wet cloth on a board on camera; watch the mark disappear.

teach.heading: What speeds it up?
teach.note: Ask: why do we spread washing out instead of leaving it in a pile?

teach.heading: Everyday evaporation
teach.note: Ask pupils for examples from home.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: 30 seconds.

check.q: Which washing dries fastest?
options: Spread out on a warm, windy day
check.why: Warmth, wind and a big surface all speed up evaporation.

practice.q: Why does a puddle dry faster on a sunny day?
practice.a: The Sun warms the water, so it evaporates faster.
practice.model:
What is different?
Sunny means warmer.
Warmth speeds up evaporation.
So the puddle dries faster.

practice.q: What does water become when it evaporates?
Name one thing other than heat that speeds up drying.

independent.q: Core: Make two wet patches with a damp cloth on a plate: one by a window, one in a shady corner. Which dries first?
independent.a: Usually the warmer place dries first.
independent.model: Teacher shows it: same cloth, same number of wipes, note the time.

independent.q: Extend: Explain your result using the word 'evaporation'.
independent.a: The patch in the warmer place dried first because water evaporates faster when it is warmer.

independent.q: Stretch: Why do clothes take longer to dry on a cold, still day?
independent.a: Low temperature and no wind mean water evaporates slowly.

exit.q: Evaporation turns a liquid into a...
exit.a: B) gas

exit.q: Big question: where does a puddle go on a sunny day?
exit.a: It evaporates into the air as water vapour.

lessons.homework: Notice three things drying at home (washing, dishes, wet hair). Write which dried fastest and why.
lessons.send: SEND: picture sequence of a drying puddle. EAL: evaporate, vapour, dry. Stretch: suggest how to test whether wind speeds up drying.

lessons.title: Fair test: what affects how fast washing dries?
lessons.bigQuestion: Does a tea towel dry faster spread out or folded up?
objectives: To understand how to plan and carry out a fair test about evaporation
successCriteria: All: make a prediction about drying
Most: keep all but one thing the same
Some: use results to say whether the prediction was right and why
lessons.crossCurricular: Maths: reading time in minutes and comparing results
lessons.smsc: Moral: honesty in recording results

keywords.def: a test where we change only one thing
what we think will happen
something that can change in a test
when a liquid turns into a gas
what the results tell us

hook.text: Two identical wet tea towels: one spread flat, one folded into a small square. Which dries first?
hook.a: The spread one: more surface for water to evaporate from.

starter.a: When a liquid turns into a gas.

starter.q: Does warmth speed up or slow down drying?
In a fair test, how many things do we change?

teach.heading: Our question
bullets: Does spreading out make drying faster?
teach.note: Write the question, then a prediction with 'because'.

teach.heading: Plan it fairly
bullets: Wet each with the same water
teach.note: Ask pupils to spot the unfair version: one cloth near a heater.

teach.heading: Example results
teach.note: Read the table together.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: 30 seconds.

check.q: Which makes the test UNFAIR?
check.why: The heater changes a second thing (temperature), so we cannot tell what caused the difference.

practice.q: Which cloth dried first in the table?
practice.model:
Read across each row to find 'dry'.
Spread out: dry at 90 minutes.
Folded: still damp at 90 minutes.
So the spread-out cloth dried first.

practice.q: Why did it dry faster?
practice.a: More of it was open to the air, so water evaporated faster.

practice.q: Name one thing kept the same.
practice.a: For example: cloth size, amount of water, place.

independent.q: Core: Do the test at home with two small cloths (one spread, one folded). Check every 30 minutes and record in your table.
independent.a: Pupils' own; the spread cloth usually dries first.
independent.model: Teacher shows the start: wet both cloths with one cup of water each, squeeze gently, place side by side.

independent.q: Extend: Write your conclusion: 'My prediction was ... because ...'
independent.a: For example: My prediction was right: the spread cloth dried first because more surface was open to the air.

independent.q: Stretch: Plan a second test to find out if wind matters. What would you change and keep the same?
independent.a: Change: wind (a fan or not); keep the same: cloth, water, how it is laid out, the room.

exit.q: A prediction is...
exit.a: A) what we think will happen

exit.q: Big question: does a tea towel dry faster spread out or folded up?
exit.a: Spread out: a bigger surface lets water evaporate faster.

lessons.homework: Finish your drying test and write your conclusion in full sentences.
lessons.send: SEND: a planning frame with 'I will change / keep the same / measure'. EAL: change, same, measure. Stretch: plan the wind test.

lessons.title: Condensation: making water appear
lessons.bigQuestion: Why does a cold can of juice get wet on the outside?
objectives: To understand that condensation is water vapour cooling and turning back into liquid water
successCriteria: All: say that condensation makes water droplets
Most: explain that the droplets come from water vapour in the air
Some: model evaporation and condensation with a cup and cling film
lessons.crossCurricular: Design and technology: why bathroom mirrors steam up and how fans help
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: noticing Allah's signs in everyday things such as dew

keywords.def: when a gas cools and turns into a liquid
water as an invisible gas
a tiny drop of liquid
make colder
a small copy that shows how something works

hook.text: The outside of a cold glass of water gets wet. The water is not leaking through. Where does it come from?
hook.a: From the air: water vapour cools on the cold glass and condenses into droplets.

starter.q: Name one thing that speeds up drying.

starter.a: A test where we change only one thing.

teach.heading: Condensation
bullets: Water vapour meets a cold surface
teach.note: Breathe on a cold mirror (or spoon from the fridge) on camera: mist appears.

teach.heading: Opposite of evaporation
teach.note: Link to the water cycle next lesson.

teach.heading: Cup and cling film model
bullets: Warm (not hot) water in a clear cup
Cling film on top, an ice cube on the film
Watch droplets form under the film
teach.note: Adult pours warm tap water. Droplets under the film: evaporation then condensation.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: 30 seconds.

check.q: Where do the drops on a cold can come from?
check.why: Water vapour in the air cools on the cold can and condenses.

practice.q: Why does a bathroom mirror steam up after a shower?
practice.a: Water vapour from the shower condenses on the cold mirror.
practice.model:
Where is the water vapour from?
The warm shower.
What does it meet?
The cold mirror.
Cooling makes vapour condense.
So droplets cover the mirror.

practice.q: Is condensation warming or cooling?
What is the opposite of condensation?

independent.q: Core: Make the cup and cling film model. After 10 minutes, draw what you see and label 'evaporation' and 'condensation'.
independent.a: Droplets under the cling film; arrows up from the water (evaporation), droplets on the film (condensation).
independent.model: Teacher shows it first: warm tap water in the cup, cover tightly, ice cube on top, wait.

independent.q: Extend: Write 3 sentences explaining what happened in your cup.
independent.a: The warm water evaporated. The vapour rose and touched the cold film. It cooled and condensed into droplets.

independent.q: Stretch: Why do car windows mist up on the inside on a cold morning?
independent.a: Warm, damp air from people's breath condenses on the cold glass.

exit.q: Condensation turns a gas into a...
exit.a: A) liquid

exit.q: Big question: why does a cold can of juice get wet on the outside?
exit.a: Water vapour in the air cools on the can and condenses into droplets.

lessons.homework: Find two places at home where condensation happens. Draw and label one.
lessons.send: SEND: a ready-labelled cup diagram to complete. EAL: condense, droplet, cool. Stretch: explain where dew on grass comes from in the morning.

lessons.unit: Spring 1: States of matter (Marvellous Medicine and How Far Can Sound Travel?)
lessons.title: The water cycle
lessons.bigQuestion: Is the water we drink today the same water that fell as rain long ago?
objectives: To understand how evaporation and condensation move water around the water cycle
successCriteria: All: put the stages of the water cycle in order
Most: name evaporation, condensation, precipitation and collection
Some: explain the role of temperature at each stage
lessons.crossCurricular: Geography: rivers, seas and rainfall
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: the water cycle as a sign of Allah's care and wisdom

keywords.def: the journey of water from land and sea to clouds and back
liquid water turning into vapour
vapour cooling into tiny droplets
water falling as rain, snow or hail
water gathering in seas, rivers and lakes

hook.text: Rain falls on mountains, runs into rivers and reaches the sea. So why does the sea not overflow?
hook.a: Water keeps evaporating from the sea, so it is always moving round the water cycle.

islamicLink.text: Allah says: 'Do you not see that Allah drives the clouds, then joins them together, then piles them up, and you see rain come out from within them?' (an-Nur 24:43). The water cycle is Allah's way of giving fresh water to the whole earth.

starter.a: A gas cooling into a liquid.

starter.q: What did you see under the cling film?

teach.heading: The cycle
bullets: Water moves in a never-ending loop
teach.note: Point to each stage in turn.
cycle: Evaporation: the Sun warms the sea

teach.heading: Up and down
teach.note: Link to the cup model: the cold cling film is like the cold air high up.

teach.heading: Order the stages
teach.note: Pupils show the order on fingers.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: 30 seconds.

check.q: Clouds form by...
check.why: Water vapour cools high up and condenses into tiny droplets: clouds.

practice.q: Put in order: condensation, collection, evaporation, precipitation.
practice.model:
Start where the Sun warms the sea: evaporation.
Vapour cools into clouds: condensation.
Rain falls: precipitation.
It gathers in rivers and seas: collection.

practice.q: What is precipitation?
practice.a: Water falling from clouds as rain, snow or hail.

practice.q: What powers the water cycle?

independent.q: Core: Draw the water cycle as a circle with 4 labelled arrows. Use all four key words.
independent.a: A labelled loop: evaporation (sea to sky), condensation (clouds), precipitation (rain), collection (rivers and sea).
independent.model: Teacher draws the first arrow: from the sea up to the sky, labelled 'evaporation: the Sun warms the water'.

independent.q: Extend: Write a short story of a water drop's journey round the cycle in 5 sentences.
independent.a: Accept a correct sequence using the four stages.
